title: Thinking in Video: Can Video Generators Really Reason About the Real World?

paper.title: Thinking in Video: Can Video Generators Really Reason About the Real World?
paper.abstract: Abstract. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal Contribution. 2 2 footnotetext: Corresponding Author. Recent advances in world models and video generation have given rise to an emerging reasoning paradigm that leverages video generative models to simulate, predict, and reason about real-world dynamics. We redefine this paradigm as Thinking in Video , where video is not merely an output artifact but a medium for constructing, extending, and verifying causal thought. However, this promise remains unverified: convincing rollouts may reflect memorized appearances rather than causal understanding, while existing metrics separate perceptual fidelity from semantic logic. To evaluate whether video generators support such reasoning, we introduce the Causal-Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ), auditing World Model Consistency from two perspectives. Explicit Causal Perception tests whether a generator reads a video scenario as a reasoning problem through spatio-temporal flattened visual question answering, while Implicit Generative Perception-Prediction Gap evaluates whether it renders the causal consequence as a consistent future video. Applying CGDJ to representative open- and closed-source generators reveals a clear Perception-Prediction Gap : open-source models produce plausible dynamics despite near-zero explicit causal perception, whereas advanced closed-source systems show stronger but still limited alignment between reasoning and generation. Further analysis exposes audio-visual misalignment, where models verbalize correct causal logic more reliably than they render it, challenging the “world simulator” narrative.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Recent progress in video generation has changed what video models appear able to do. Autoregressive and diffusion-based systems now synthesize high-definition, minute-long clips with coherent objects, motions, and interactions ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Blattmann et al., 2023 ; OpenAI, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Google, 2025 ; Wan et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . This leap motivates a claim beyond visual synthesis: if a model can roll out plausible futures from visual conditions, it may use video as a medium for reasoning. We call this direction Thinking in Video : instead of merely describing answers in language, the model constructs, extends, and audits a visual world over time. Video generators thus become candidate General World Simulators , internalizing the physical laws and social dynamics that govern reality across diverse scenarios ( Ali et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2025 ; Bansal et al., 2025 ) . Recent attempts at “thinking with video” explore this possibility for mathematics, navigation, and embodied problem solving ( Li et al., 2022 ; Tong et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025a ; Chow et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025a ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . However, the central promise of Thinking in Video remains unverified. A convincing rollout is not necessarily a correct reasoning process. A model may generate shattering glass, a falling object, or a human response because it understands causal conditions or memorized high-frequency visual associations ( Liu et al., 2024a ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . The distinction matters: reasoning requires counterfactual and causal validity, not photorealistic continuation alone. Existing evaluation often rewards perceptual quality through Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) or Inception Score, while ignoring whether the generated future obeys scene mechanics ( Salimans et al., 2016 ; Unterthiner et al., 2019 ; Ge et al., 2024 ) . Without separating visual plausibility from causal correctness, treating video generators as reasoning engines for open-world decision making is premature ( Gupta et al., 2024 ; Somepalli et al., 2023 ; Valmeekam et al., 2023 ; Motamed et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . Existing benchmarks rarely test whether a model can understand a causal situation and act through generation. This reflects a structural deficiency: paradigms bifurcate visual fidelity from semantic logic. Distributional metrics measure smoothness, realism, or text alignment, yet hallucinations may score well ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Brooks et al., 2024 ; Le et al., 2025 ) . Static multimodal benchmarks probe symbolic or visual question-answering, but not evolving video answers ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Rawte et al., 2025 ) . Thus, when a generator seems to reason, we cannot tell whether it simulates causality or imitates appearances. This gap hides Perception-Prediction Dissonance : a model may know the outcome yet fail to render consistent pixels. Evaluating Thinking in Video requires auditing perception and prediction across physical and social dynamics ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; LeCun, 2022 ; Li et al., 2025a ) . To close this gap, as shown in Figure 1 , we introduce the Causal-Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ), a benchmark and evaluation framework for assessing whether video generative models can truly Think in Video . Rather than asking only whether the output looks good, CGDJ asks whether the model can use video as a reasoning medium: it must recognize causal structure from visual evidence and then ground that structure by generating a valid temporal consequence. The paradigm contains two complementary modules: ❶ Explicit Causal Perception : We test whether a model can identify and articulate a video’s causal structure, rather than merely generate a plausible continuation. Since most video generators cannot process interleaved video-text prompts, our Flatten Temporal Video strategy converts video frames and rasterized queries into a unified image grid. This creates an explicit, directly judgeable visual QA task, forcing the model to reveal its recognized causal progression instead of relying on statistical continuation. ❷ Implicit Generative Prediction : We test whether a model can enact its reasoning in video. Conditioned on a causal antecedent, the model must synthesize the consequent future sequence. This generative protocol forces the model to move beyond choosing or verbalizing an answer: it must physically render the outcome, enabling direct inspection of whether its visual rollout is causally valid. Experiments reveal that current video generators are only partially capable of Thinking in Video . On the explicit side, advanced closed-source generators such as Sora-2 and Veo-3.1 show measurable causal perception, whereas open-source generators nearly collapse under the same flattened reasoning protocol. On the generative side, however, open-source models can still produce moderately plausible causal continuations, exposing a sharp Perception-Prediction Gap : visual action can surpass explicit causal understanding. Further analysis shows an audio-visual misalignment where models often articulate the correct causal logic more reliably than they render it. These results challenge a simple “world simulator” narrative. Current systems can imitate parts of world dynamics, and the strongest models begin to align perception with prediction, but robust video-based reasoning still requires stronger grounding between causal knowledge and visual computation. Our key contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We redefine reasoning with video generative models as the Thinking in Video paradigm, where video becomes a medium for constructing and verifying causal thought, and highlight the need to properly evaluate whether current generators can support such reasoning. (2) We propose the Causal-Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ) framework, with the Flatten Temporal Video strategy, to jointly evaluate Explicit Causal Perception and Implicit Generative Prediction in current video generative models. (3) Through experiments, we reveal a fundamental Perception-Prediction Gap: current models can exhibit plausible visual dynamics without reliable causal perception, while advanced systems show early but still limited alignment between explicit reasoning and generative simulation. To facilitate further research, all code and data will be publicly available: https://github.com/BRZ911/Thinking-in-Video . Figure 2 . The construction process of the CGDJ benchmark. sections.heading: 2. Causal–Generative Dual-Judge
sections.text: To evaluate whether video generative models are simply mimicking pixel statistics or truly simulating world dynamics, we propose the Causal–Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ) . As shown in Figure 2 , this paradigm decouples the evaluation of semantic comprehension ( Perception ) from physical rendering ( Prediction ). CGDJ consists of: (i) Causal–Generative Dual-Judge Benchmark ( § ​ 2.1 \lx@sectionsign\ref{sec:benchmark} ), and (ii) Causal–Generative Dual-Judge Evaluation .

sections.heading: 2.1.1. Explicit Causal Understanding Data
sections.text: As shown in Figure 2 (a), the comprehensive benchmark construction process consists of two main phases: Data Collection and Flatten Temporal Video Transition : Data Collection. To evaluate the causal reasoning of video generative models, we align our benchmark with video understanding standards by adopting all 900 videos from Video-MME ( Fu et al., 2025 ) . To ensure a comprehensive evaluation across different temporal scales, the collection spans short, medium, and long durations. Furthermore, the dataset covers a diverse range of real-world dynamics, categorized into six domains: (i) Knowledge , (ii) Life Record , (iii) Sports Competition , (iv) Artistic Performance , (v) Film & Television , and (vi) Multilingual . The statistical distribution across these individual domains is presented in Figure 3 (a). This enables evaluating causal internalization across diverse physical and social dynamics. Flatten Temporal Video Transition. Since current video generative models are strictly restricted to processing only static image inputs, to overcome this fundamental limitation, we propose the Flatten Temporal Video strategy that maps a video-question pair onto a single static image I composite ∈ ℝ 720 × 1280 × 3 I_{\text{composite}}\in\mathbb{R}^{720\times 1280\times 3} . Formally, given a video 𝒱 \mathcal{V} and a question-option pair 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} , the construction process consists of three steps: 1. Temporal Grid Construction: We extract a sequence of N = 70 N=70 frames through uniform temporal sampling. These frames are concatenated into a spatial matrix I grid I_{\text{grid}} with dimensions 7 × 10 7\times 10 : (1) I grid = ⊕ r = 1 7 ​ ( ⊕ c = 1 10 ​ x t ( r − 1 ) ​ 10 + c ) I_{\text{grid}}=\underset{r=1}{\overset{7}{\oplus}}\left(\underset{c=1}{\overset{10}{\oplus}}x_{t_{(r-1)10+c}}\right) where ⊕ \oplus denotes spatial concatenation. This grid effectively transforms the temporal sequence into a spatial texture accessible to the visual encoder. 2. Semantic Rendering: Instead of relying on conventional pre-trained external text encoders, we directly transform the specific textual query 𝒬 \mathcal{Q} into a dense pixel-space representation I text I_{\text{text}} via a dedicated high-fidelity rasterization function. This newly rendered text block is strategically positioned to occupy the entire upper spatial visual field of the final image grid. 3. Vertical Integration: The final composite input for the model is meticulously synthesized by vertically concatenating the specific semantic instruction tensor and the flattened temporal grid tensor along the primary height dimension. In order to ensure full technical compatibility with existing standard video generation architectures, this newly fused tensor subsequently undergoes an adaptive resizing operation to match the required target resolution: (2) I composite = Resize 1280 × 720 ​ ( [ I text ; I grid ] ) I_{\text{composite}}=\text{Resize}_{1280\times 720}([I_{\text{text}};I_{\text{grid}}]) This layout creates a “visual representation” by stacking text above the grid, enabling causal reasoning through joint attention to instructions and history.

sections.heading: 2.1.2. Implicit Generative Action Data
sections.text: As shown in Figure 2 (b), the construction process consists of three main steps: Data Collection , Video Splitting , and Flattening of Temporal Video Transitions :

sections.heading: Data Collection.
sections.text: We systematically classify the broad spectrum of World Dynamics into Natural Sciences and Sociology & Humanities , balancing the evaluation between rigid physical mechanics and complex human behaviors. • Natural Sciences: This category evaluates the model’s fundamental understanding of physical laws. We aggregate data from various authoritative benchmarks including The Sound of Water ( Bagad et al., 2025 ) , Physion ( Bear et al., 2021 ) , and Physics IQ Benchmark ( Motamed et al., 2026 ) . We classify these into four fine-grained sub-domains: (i) Physical Mechanics , (ii) Natural & Life Sciences , (iii) Materials & Structures , and (iv) Fields & Energy . • Sociology & Humanities: This category evaluates the simulation of human behaviors and social logic. Data sources include the TLD Benchmark (Vehicle Signals) ( Chai et al., 2024 ) , Kinetics Human Action ( Kay et al., 2017 ) , Ego4D ( Grauman et al., 2022 ) , and selected web videos. These are categorized into sub-domains: (i) Transportation Behavior , (ii) Life Behavior , (iii) Occupational Role Behavior , (iv) Public Social Behavior , and (v) Sports Activity Behavior . As shown in Figure 3 (b), the final curated benchmark comprises a total of 600 high-quality videos. To ensure an unbiased evaluation between physical rigidity and social complexity, we maintain a strictly balanced distribution across the two domains: 300 samples for Natural Sciences and 300 samples for Sociology & Humanities .

sections.heading: Video Splitting.
sections.text: To rigorously reformulate the standard generative task as a structured causal prediction problem, we implement a precise temporal segmentation strategy. For every video in the benchmark, expert annotators manually identify and pinpoint the Causal Inflection Point (or critical node). This specific timestamp represents the definitive boundary where the accumulation of causal conditions triggers an irreversible event or state transition. ❶ Input Video: The pre-event sequence serves as the visual condition, providing the necessary causal context for the subsequent generation. Furthermore, we use Gemini-3-Pro ( Team et al., 2025b ) to produce a detailed semantic video description, which is co-injected with the video to facilitate the generation. ❷ Gold Video: The subsequent temporal segment functions as the immutable ground truth reference, capturing the realized outcome of the initial conditions. This empirically recorded footage serves as a rigorous baseline to audit the validity of the model’s extrapolation.

sections.heading: Flattening of Temporal Video Transitions.
sections.text: Similar to the previously mentioned strategy in the Explicit Understanding module, we employ a flattening technique to input the video context into the generative model. Specifically, we extract N = 7 N=7 keyframes from the Input Video at uniform discrete temporal steps to represent the motion trajectory. Formally, these frames are spatially concatenated to form a continuous visual condition I motion I_{\text{motion}} : (3) I motion = ⊕ i = 1 𝑁 ​ x t i I_{\text{motion}}=\underset{i=1}{\overset{N}{\oplus}}x_{t_{i}} where x t i x_{t_{i}} represents the frame at time step t i t_{i} and ⊕ \oplus denotes spatial horizontal concatenation. sections.heading: 2.2. Causal–Generative Dual-Judge Evaluation
sections.text: To quantify the capabilities of the model in simulating world dynamics, as shown in Figure 4 , we design an automated evaluation pipeline based on advanced multimodal models. Figure 4 . The overall evaluation pipeline of the Causal–Generative Dual-Judge consists of two distinct yet complementary protocols: (a) Explicit Causal Understanding Evaluation and (b) Implicit Generative Action Evaluation .

sections.heading: 2.2.1. Explicit Causal Evaluation
sections.text: To assess causal validity through reasoning, as shown in Figure 4 (a), we establish a robust, comprehensive, and fully automated two-stage framework: Audio-Text Alignment and MLLM-based Causal Adjudication .

sections.heading: Audio Context Extraction.
sections.text: The generated videos often contain the correct solution or reasoning steps encoded directly within the audio. To strictly evaluate this verbal information, we utilize the whisper-large-v2 ( Radford et al., 2023 ) model to extract and transcribe the audio track. By converting the spoken problem-solving process into text, we ensure that the judge considers both the visual outcome and the model’s narrated logic for a more holistic assessment.

sections.heading: MLLM-based Adjudication.
sections.text: We employ the Gemini-3-Pro ( Team et al., 2025b ) as the core evaluator, owing to its superior video understanding and long-context reasoning capabilities critical for our analysis. Specifically, the evaluation process functions as follows: ❶ Input Construction: We construct a composite prompt for Gemini, which includes the following key inputs: (1) the Generated Video produced by the model under test, (2) the Transcribed Audio Text , (3) the Original Question and Option , and (4) the Ground Truth Answer . ❷ Causal Judgment: Gemini-3-Pro is tasked to act as a judge. It compares the visual events in the generated video against the logical requirements of the correct answer. The MLLM determines whether the generated video depicts the causal consequence implied by ground truth, classifying the generation as “Correct” or “Incorrect” . We validate this automated metric against human judgment in Figure 6 . This automated pipeline ensures that the evaluation moves beyond superficial pixel metrics and focuses on the semantic and causal correctness of the generated content.

sections.heading: 2.2.2. Implicit Generative Evaluation
sections.text: To evaluate the real-world simulation authenticity, as shown in Figure 4 (b), we employ a comprehensive, systematic, and rigorous Reference-Based Comparative Evaluation . Using Gemini-3-Pro effectively serves as a dedicated “Video Quality Auditor”. It systematically benchmarks the video generated by the model against the ground truth “Gold Video”, while ensuring strict adherence to the governing textual description.

sections.heading: Scoring Mechanism.
sections.text: The automated evaluator assigns a score S ∈ [ 0.0 , 1.0 ] S\in[0.0,1.0] based on the following three dimensions: (i) Semantic Alignment (object/action correctness), (ii) Reference Consistency (logical flow vs. ground truth), and (iii) Physical Validity (absence of flickering/physics violations). Scores range from 0.0 0.0 (hallucinations) to 1.0 1.0 (perfect match), effectively quantifying the model’s innate ability to ground reasoning into physical action.

sections.heading: 3. Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we conduct a comprehensive empirical analysis to validate the newly proposed Causal–Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ). Our systematic experiments are structured to probe the two most distinct facets of world simulation: (1) Explicit Causal Understanding: We first assess whether various models possess the essential theoretical knowledge to identify correct causal dynamics governing complex real-world events through specific analytical tasks. (2) Implicit Generative Action: We then evaluate the intrinsic ability of the video generation models to physically ground this knowledge by generating valid future video sequences that closely align with real-world dynamics. By comparing these two complementary modalities, we aim to further quantify the “Perception-Prediction Gap” and diagnose the state of modern video generative models as world simulators.

sections.heading: 3.1. Experimental Setup for Explicit Causal Understanding
sections.text: To evaluate the explicit reasoning capabilities of video generative models, we benchmark them against advanced MLLMs to quantitatively highlight the critical perception and reasoning performance gap. The experimental setup is designed as follows:

sections.heading: Multimodal Large Language Model Baselines.
sections.text: To establish a performance ceiling and validate the effectiveness of our visual representation, we evaluate a suite of advanced MLLMs. This includes Qwen3-VL-Instruct (2B, 4B, and 8B) ( Bai et al., 2025 ) , as well as proprietary frontier models including GPT-5 ( Singh et al., 2025 ) and Gemini-3-Flash ( Team et al., 2025b ) . For these MLLMs, we design two distinct input protocols to analyze the impact of information formatting: (1) Setting A (Native Video Input): The models process the original video tokens directly, utilizing their native temporal encoders. (2) Setting B (Flatten Temporal Video Input): The models process the “flattened” spatial grid image (as described in § ​ 2.1 \lx@sectionsign\ref{sec:benchmark} ), identical to the input format used for video generative models. sections.heading: 3.2. Main Results
sections.text: Table 2 and Table 3 summarize the quantitative results of our Causal–Generative Dual-Judge evaluation. From these experimental comparisons, we observe that: 1. Spatio-Temporal Flattening serves as a valid medium for causal reasoning. To validate whether our flattening strategy preserves sufficient information for reasoning, we compare MLLM performance under Native versus Flatten Temporal Video Input. The results show that while transforming temporal videos into spatial grids naturally causes some information loss, advanced MLLMs maintain robust performance. Notably, Gemini-3-Flash achieves 74.1% under the flattened setting, retaining approximately 89% of its native performance ( 83.0% ). Even the smaller Qwen3-VL-8B maintains a respectable 81% relative to its native performance. This evidence confirms that the “visual medium” constructed by our flattening technique contains sufficient logical cues. 2. Emergent but Limited Reasoning in Generative Models. A distinct divide emerges. Closed-source models such as Sora-2 ( 51.2% ) and Veo-3.1 ( 49.9% ) exhibit measurable explicit reasoning capabilities, performing on par with an 8B-parameter MLLM. This suggests that scaling video generation, or internal prompt rewriting pipelines, fosters an emergent, albeit rudimentary, understanding of world dynamics. However, they significantly trail behind state-of-the-art reasoning engines, Gemini-3-Flash at 74.1%, indicating that current “World Simulators” are not yet robust reasoners. Notably, open-weights models like Wan-2.2 ( 0.7% ) and HunyuanVideo ( 1.5% ) suffer a complete collapse in this discriminative task, likely due to a lack of instruction-following alignment in their training. 3. Closed-Source Models Dominate Physical Simulation. In the generative domain, Sora-2 leads with an average score of 61.6% , followed closely by Veo-3.1 ( 58.9% ), demonstrating superior capability in simulating complex dynamics. Open-source models lag behind at 42.5% and 41.5% under our automated MLLM evaluation. Interestingly, models consistently perform better in Sociology & Humanities, Sora-2: 65.6%, than in Natural Sciences, Sora-2: 57.7% . This divergence suggests that the rigid, immutable laws of physics governing the real world may present a more formidable challenge for models to internalize than the patterns of social dynamics. 4. Advanced Mimicry vs. True Understanding. By juxtaposing Table 2 and Table 3 , we uncover a critical “Perception-Prediction Gap” that distinguishes advanced mimicry from true understanding. A striking dissonance is observed in open-weights models like Wan-2.2 , which achieves a respectable competency in Implicit Generative Action ( 41.5% ) despite a near-zero score in Explicit Understanding ( 0.7% ). This implies that such models operate via statistical pixel mimicry, rendering the texture of causal events without comprehending the underlying logic. In contrast, Sora-2 demonstrates a synchronized profile (Explicit: 51.2% , Implicit: 61.6% ). This correlation suggests that as models scale towards authentic “World Simulators,” their generative actions become increasingly grounded in an explicit grasp of causal laws, marking the transition from surface-level synthesis to physically consistent simulation. sections.heading: 3.3. Causal–Generative Dual-Judge Analysis
sections.text: To gain deeper insights into the underlying mechanisms of the “Perception-Prediction Gap” and address potential formatting confounders, we conduct a series of in-depth analytical experiments. 1. The Disconnect Between Linguistic Knowledge and Generative Action. To deeply diagnose the “Perception-Prediction Gap”, we evaluate the consistency between the model’s verbal output and visual output under identical input conditions . Specifically, we assess the generation accuracy across two distinct channels: the Audio-Only (whether the model verbally articulates the correct reasoning/answer) and the Video-Only (whether the model physically renders the correct reasoning). The results shown in Figure 5 , the comparative results reveal a striking Audio-Visual Misalignment independent of instruction-following recognition accuracy. We observe that the accuracy of Audio generation significantly surpasses that of Video generation. This indicates that the model has successfully internalized the Semantic Knowledge necessary to describe the causal outcome, proving it theoretically “understands” the scenario. However, this semantic comprehension fails to transfer into Physical Grounding . The model acts as a “theoretical expert but practical novice”, capable of verbally predicting the future but incapable of simulating the pixel-level dynamics. This result demonstrates that current models rely on linguistic priors to solve problems, rather than operating on a robust internal world model. Figure 5 . Comparison of Audio ∩ \cap Video , Video-Only and Audio-Only . The empirical results show that Audio accuracy consistently surpasses Video accuracy by a significant margin. This indicates models can semantically describe outcomes but fail to physically generate them. 2. Validation of Automated Scoring via Human Alignment. To validate the reliability of our Gemini-3-Pro evaluator, we conduct a Human Evaluation Alignment study. Three human experts blindly rate the test set, and we compute their average scores to benchmark physical and consistency. The result, as shown in Figure 6 , comparing their consensus scores against the model’s predictions reveals a high degree of concordance. We achieve a Pearson Correlation of 0.8205 and a Mean Absolute Difference of 0.1468 . These metrics confirm that Gemini-3-Pro mirrors human judgment, serving as a robust agent for evaluation. Figure 6 . Alignment analysis between Gemini-3-Pro Ratings (Blue) and Human Expert Ratings (Green) on the Implicit Generative Action task. The plot illustrates the score distribution across video samples. With a high Pearson Correlation of 0.82 and a low Mean Absolute Difference of 0.14 . 3. The Trade-off Between Temporal Density and Spatial Resolution. To validate the optimal sampling strategy for the Flatten Temporal Video , we evaluate the reasoning capacity under varying temporal granularities. The results are as follows: Figure 7 . The bar chart and table illustrate the Explicit Causal Understanding accuracy for Veo-3.1 and Sora-2 under three specific flattening strategies: 5 × 8 5\times 8 (sparse), 7 × 10 7\times 10 (balanced), and 8 × 12 8\times 12 (dense). The 7 × 10 7\times 10 setting yields the optimal average performance across all categories. Figure 8 . Performance comparison across varying inputs for the action task. The results demonstrate that the 7-Pics yields the highest fidelity, outperforming both sparse and dense contexts by achieving an optimal balance. ❶ Explicit Causal Understanding (5 × \times 8 vs. 7 × \times 10 vs. 8 × \times 12): As shown in Figure 7 , the results reveal a distinct inverted-U performance curve across most durations, peaking at our default 7 × 10 7\times 10 configuration. Notably, increasing density to 8 × 12 8\times 12 causes a performance drop (e.g., Veo-3.1 falls from 49.9 % 49.9\% to 43.4 % 43.4\% , while Sora-2 drops to 47.4 % 47.4\% ). This suggests that while more frames theoretically offer richer temporal context, they induce severe Visual Compression that hinders semantic extraction from the dense grid due to reduced cell resolution. Furthermore, while the 5 × 8 5\times 8 layout benefits short clips, it lacks the necessary temporal resolution required for complex causal reasoning in longer sequences. ❷ Implicit Generative Action (1 vs. 4 vs. 7 vs. 10 Pics): As shown in Figure 8 , comparing the results confirms that 7-pics represent the optimal prompt, outperforming both sparse (1, 4 pics) and dense (10 pics) inputs. The lower scores at fewer frames suggest Motion Ambiguity , where the model lacks sufficient temporal vectors to extrapolate future states. Conversely, the slight decline at 10 frames points to Contextual Redundancy where highly compressed keyframes introduce spatial noise that overwhelms the visual encoder’s semantic feature extraction. In summary, these findings confirm that our chosen configurations ( 7 × 10 7\times 10 grid and 7 frames) strike the optimal balance between preserving spatial fidelity and encoding sufficient temporal dynamics required for robust simulation.

sections.heading: 4. Related Work
sections.text: Towards “Thinking with Video”. Recent advancements in Video Generation Model have evolved beyond high-fidelity texture synthesis toward complex spatiotemporal dynamics modeling ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ) . This progression supports the conceptualization of video generators as nascent general world simulators and promotes the “thinking with video” paradigm, where generation functions as an intrinsic component of reasoning ( Tong et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025b ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . However, distinguishing genuine causal understanding from mere statistical memorization remains a pivotal challenge, as traditional metrics disproportionately favor perceptual fidelity over logical consistency. The Gap in Existing Reasoning Benchmarks. Emerging benchmarks evaluate various reasoning facets, ranging from rule-based dynamics ( He et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) to open-ended visual reasoning ( Qin et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) and specific tasks ( Yang et al., 2025a ) . While recent efforts attempt to mitigate appearance biases ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Deng, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Cai et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . However, relying on rudimentary tasks, they fail to verify physical and social dynamics. By evaluating discrimination and generation in isolation, they overlook the gap between surface-level outputs and genuine causal understanding. To address the critical gap in current causal evaluation and in contrast to existing methods, we introduce the Causal–Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ) framework. Unlike previous works, CGDJ jointly evaluates internal consistency through two complementary modalities, Explicit Causal Understanding and Implicit Generative Action . By constructing the Causal–Generative Evaluation Benchmark, we provide a rigorous testbed to distinguish whether video generative models have genuinely internalized the physical laws and causal structures governing the scenes they render.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
sections.text: We redefine reasoning with video generative models as Thinking in Video and introduce the Causal-Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ) to evaluate whether current generators can support this paradigm. By jointly examining Explicit Causal Perception and Implicit Generative Prediction , we reveal a clear Perception-Prediction Gap : models may generate plausible visual dynamics without reliable causal perception, while stronger systems show early but limited alignment between reasoning and generation. We further identify audio-visual misalignment, where verbalized causal knowledge does not necessarily translate into consistent video rollouts. Ultimately, CGDJ advocates shifting video generation evaluation from perceptual fidelity toward causal consistency, offering diagnostic insights for grounded, reasoning-capable world models.

Recent advances in world models and video generation have given rise to an emerging reasoning paradigm that leverages video generative models to simulate, predict, and reason about real-world dynamics. We redefine this paradigm as Thinking in Video , where video is not merely an output artifact but a medium for constructing, extending, and verifying causal thought. However, this promise remains unverified: convincing rollouts may reflect memorized appearances rather than causal understanding, while existing metrics separate perceptual fidelity from semantic logic. To evaluate whether video generators support such reasoning, we introduce the Causal-Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ), auditing World Model Consistency from two perspectives. Explicit Causal Perception tests whether a generator reads a video scenario as a reasoning problem through spatio-temporal flattened visual question answering, while Implicit Generative Perception-Prediction Gap evaluates whether it renders the causal consequence as a consistent future video. Applying CGDJ to representative open- and closed-source generators reveals a clear Perception-Prediction Gap : open-source models produce plausible dynamics despite near-zero explicit causal perception, whereas advanced closed-source systems show stronger but still limited alignment between reasoning and generation. Further analysis exposes audio-visual misalignment, where models verbalize correct causal logic more reliably than they render it, challenging the “world simulator” narrative. Keywords: World Models, Video Generative Models, Thinking in Video. 1. Introduction Recent progress in video generation has changed what video models appear able to do. Autoregressive and diffusion-based systems now synthesize high-definition, minute-long clips with coherent objects, motions, and interactions ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Blattmann et al., 2023 ; OpenAI, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Google, 2025 ; Wan et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . This leap motivates a claim beyond visual synthesis: if a model can roll out plausible futures from visual conditions, it may use video as a medium for reasoning. We call this direction Thinking in Video : instead of merely describing answers in language, the model constructs, extends, and audits a visual world over time. Video generators thus become candidate General World Simulators , internalizing the physical laws and social dynamics that govern reality across diverse scenarios ( Ali et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2025 ; Bansal et al., 2025 ) . Recent attempts at “thinking with video” explore this possibility for mathematics, navigation, and embodied problem solving ( Li et al., 2022 ; Tong et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025a ; Chow et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025a ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . However, the central promise of Thinking in Video remains unverified. A convincing rollout is not necessarily a correct reasoning process. A model may generate shattering glass, a falling object, or a human response because it understands causal conditions or memorized high-frequency visual associations ( Liu et al., 2024a ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . The distinction matters: reasoning requires counterfactual and causal validity, not photorealistic continuation alone. Existing evaluation often rewards perceptual quality through Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) or Inception Score, while ignoring whether the generated future obeys scene mechanics ( Salimans et al., 2016 ; Unterthiner et al., 2019 ; Ge et al., 2024 ) . Without separating visual plausibility from causal correctness, treating video generators as reasoning engines for open-world decision making is premature ( Gupta et al., 2024 ; Somepalli et al., 2023 ; Valmeekam et al., 2023 ; Motamed et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . Existing benchmarks rarely test whether a model can understand a causal situation and act through generation. This reflects a structural deficiency: paradigms bifurcate visual fidelity from semantic logic. Distributional metrics measure smoothness, realism, or text alignment, yet hallucinations may score well ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Brooks et al., 2024 ; Le et al., 2025 ) . Static multimodal benchmarks probe symbolic or visual question-answering, but not evolving video answers ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Rawte et al., 2025 ) . Thus, when a generator seems to reason, we cannot tell whether it simulates causality or imitates appearances. This gap hides Perception-Prediction Dissonance : a model may know the outcome yet fail to render consistent pixels. Evaluating Thinking in Video requires auditing perception and prediction across physical and social dynamics ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; LeCun, 2022 ; Li et al., 2025a ) . To close this gap, as shown in Figure 1 , we introduce the Causal-Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ), a benchmark and evaluation framework for assessing whether video generative models can truly Think in Video . Rather than asking only whether the output looks good, CGDJ asks whether the model can use video as a reasoning medium: it must recognize causal structure from visual evidence and then ground that structure by generating a valid temporal consequence. The paradigm contains two complementary modules: ❶ Explicit Causal Perception : We test whether a model can identify and articulate a video’s causal structure, rather than merely generate a plausible continuation. Since most video generators cannot process interleaved video-text prompts, our Flatten Temporal Video strategy converts video frames and rasterized queries into a unified image grid. This creates an explicit, directly judgeable visual QA task, forcing the model to reveal its recognized causal progression instead of relying on statistical continuation. ❷ Implicit Generative Prediction : We test whether a model can enact its reasoning in video. Conditioned on a causal antecedent, the model must synthesize the consequent future sequence. This generative protocol forces the model to move beyond choosing or verbalizing an answer: it must physically render the outcome, enabling direct inspection of whether its visual rollout is causally valid. Experiments reveal that current video generators are only partially capable of Thinking in Video . On the explicit side, advanced closed-source generators such as Sora-2 and Veo-3.1 show measurable causal perception, whereas open-source generators nearly collapse under the same flattened reasoning protocol. On the generative side, however, open-source models can still produce moderately plausible causal continuations, exposing a sharp Perception-Prediction Gap : visual action can surpass explicit causal understanding. Further analysis shows an audio-visual misalignment where models often articulate the correct causal logic more reliably than they render it. These results challenge a simple “world simulator” narrative. Current systems can imitate parts of world dynamics, and the strongest models begin to align perception with prediction, but robust video-based reasoning still requires stronger grounding between causal knowledge and visual computation. Our key contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We redefine reasoning with video generative models as the Thinking in Video paradigm, where video becomes a medium for constructing and verifying causal thought, and highlight the need to properly evaluate whether current generators can support such reasoning. (2) We propose the Causal-Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ) framework, with the Flatten Temporal Video strategy, to jointly evaluate Explicit Causal Perception and Implicit Generative Prediction in current video generative models. (3) Through experiments, we reveal a fundamental Perception-Prediction Gap: current models can exhibit plausible visual dynamics without reliable causal perception, while advanced systems show early but still limited alignment between explicit reasoning and generative simulation. Causal–Generative Dual-Judge To evaluate whether video generative models are simply mimicking pixel statistics or truly simulating world dynamics, we propose the Causal–Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ) . As shown in Figure 2 , this paradigm decouples the evaluation of semantic comprehension ( Perception ) from physical rendering ( Prediction ). Implicit Generative Action Data As shown in Figure 2 (b), the construction process consists of three main steps: Data Collection , Video Splitting , and Flattening of Temporal Video Transitions : Data Collection. We systematically classify the broad spectrum of World Dynamics into Natural Sciences and Sociology & Humanities , balancing the evaluation between rigid physical mechanics and complex human behaviors. • Natural Sciences: This category evaluates the model’s fundamental understanding of physical laws. We aggregate data from various authoritative benchmarks including The Sound of Water ( Bagad et al., 2025 ) , Physion ( Bear et al., 2021 ) , and Physics IQ Benchmark ( Motamed et al., 2026 ) . We classify these into four fine-grained sub-domains: (i) Physical Mechanics , (ii) Natural & Life Sciences , (iii) Materials & Structures , and (iv) Fields & Energy . • Sociology & Humanities: This category evaluates the simulation of human behaviors and social logic. Data sources include the TLD Benchmark (Vehicle Signals) ( Chai et al., 2024 ) , Kinetics Human Action ( Kay et al., 2017 ) , Ego4D ( Grauman et al., 2022 ) , and selected web videos. These are categorized into sub-domains: (i) Transportation Behavior , (ii) Life Behavior , (iii) Occupational Role Behavior , (iv) Public Social Behavior , and (v) Sports Activity Behavior . As shown in Figure 3 (b), the final curated benchmark comprises a total of 600 high-quality videos. To ensure an unbiased evaluation between physical rigidity and social complexity, we maintain a strictly balanced distribution across the two domains: 300 samples for Natural Sciences and 300 samples for Sociology & Humanities . Video Splitting. To rigorously reformulate the standard generative task as a structured causal prediction problem, we implement a precise temporal segmentation strategy. For every video in the benchmark, expert annotators manually identify and pinpoint the Causal Inflection Point (or critical node). This specific timestamp represents the definitive boundary where the accumulation of causal conditions triggers an irreversible event or state transition. ❶ Input Video: The pre-event sequence serves as the visual condition, providing the necessary causal context for the subsequent generation. Causal–Generative Dual-Judge Evaluation To quantify the capabilities of the model in simulating world dynamics, as shown in Figure 4 , we design an automated evaluation pipeline based on advanced multimodal models. Figure 4 . The overall evaluation pipeline of the Causal–Generative Dual-Judge consists of two distinct yet complementary protocols: (a) Explicit Causal Understanding Evaluation and (b) Implicit Generative Action Evaluation . 2.2.1. Explicit Causal Evaluation To assess causal validity through reasoning, as shown in Figure 4 (a), we establish a robust, comprehensive, and fully automated two-stage framework: Audio-Text Alignment and MLLM-based Causal Adjudication . Audio Context Extraction. The generated videos often contain the correct solution or reasoning steps encoded directly within the audio. To strictly evaluate this verbal information, we utilize the whisper-large-v2 ( Radford et al., 2023 ) model to extract and transcribe the audio track. By converting the spoken problem-solving process into text, we ensure that the judge considers both the visual outcome and the model’s narrated logic for a more holistic assessment. MLLM-based Adjudication. We employ the Gemini-3-Pro ( Team et al., 2025b ) as the core evaluator, owing to its superior video understanding and long-context reasoning capabilities critical for our analysis. Specifically, the evaluation process functions as follows: ❶ Input Construction: We construct a composite prompt for Gemini, which includes the following key inputs: (1) the Generated Video produced by the model under test, (2) the Transcribed Audio Text , (3) the Original Question and Option , and (4) the Ground Truth Answer . ❷ Causal Judgment: Gemini-3-Pro is tasked to act as a judge. It compares the visual events in the generated video against the logical requirements of the correct answer. The MLLM determines whether the generated video depicts the causal consequence implied by ground truth, classifying the generation as “Correct” or “Incorrect” . We validate this automated metric against human judgment in Figure 6 . This automated pipeline ensures that the evaluation moves beyond superficial pixel metrics and focuses on the semantic and causal correctness of the generated content. 2.2.2. Implicit Generative Evaluation To evaluate the real-world simulation authenticity, as shown in Figure 4 (b), we employ a comprehensive, systematic, and rigorous Reference-Based Comparative Evaluation . Using Gemini-3-Pro effectively serves as a dedicated “Video Quality Auditor”. It systematically benchmarks the video generated by the model against the ground truth “Gold Video”, while ensuring strict adherence to the governing textual description. Scoring Mechanism. The automated evaluator assigns a score S ∈ [ 0.0 , 1.0 ] S\in[0.0,1.0] based on the following three dimensions: (i) Semantic Alignment (object/action correctness), (ii) Reference Consistency (logical flow vs. ground truth), and (iii) Physical Validity (absence of flickering/physics violations). Scores range from 0.0 0.0 (hallucinations) to 1.0 1.0 (perfect match), effectively quantifying the model’s innate ability to ground reasoning into physical action. 3. Experiments In this section, we conduct a comprehensive empirical analysis to validate the newly proposed Causal–Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ). Our systematic experiments are structured to probe the two most distinct facets of world simulation: (1) Explicit Causal Understanding: We first assess whether various models possess the essential theoretical knowledge to identify correct causal dynamics governing complex real-world events through specific analytical tasks. (2) Implicit Generative Action: We then evaluate the intrinsic ability of the video generation models to physically ground this knowledge by generating valid future video sequences that closely align with real-world dynamics. By comparing these two complementary modalities, we aim to further quantify the “Perception-Prediction Gap” and diagnose the state of modern video generative models as world simulators. 3.1. Main Results Table 2 and Table 3 summarize the quantitative results of our Causal–Generative Dual-Judge evaluation. From these experimental comparisons, we observe that: 1. Spatio-Temporal Flattening serves as a valid medium for causal reasoning. To validate whether our flattening strategy preserves sufficient information for reasoning, we compare MLLM performance under Native versus Flatten Temporal Video Input. The results show that while transforming temporal videos into spatial grids naturally causes some information loss, advanced MLLMs maintain robust performance. Notably, Gemini-3-Flash achieves 74.1% under the flattened setting, retaining approximately 89% of its native performance ( 83.0% ). Even the smaller Qwen3-VL-8B maintains a respectable 81% relative to its native performance. This evidence confirms that the “visual medium” constructed by our flattening technique contains sufficient logical cues. 2. Emergent but Limited Reasoning in Generative Models. A distinct divide emerges. Closed-source models such as Sora-2 ( 51.2% ) and Veo-3.1 ( 49.9% ) exhibit measurable explicit reasoning capabilities, performing on par with an 8B-parameter MLLM. This suggests that scaling video generation, or internal prompt rewriting pipelines, fosters an emergent, albeit rudimentary, understanding of world dynamics. However, they significantly trail behind state-of-the-art reasoning engines, Gemini-3-Flash at 74.1%, indicating that current “World Simulators” are not yet robust reasoners. Notably, open-weights models like Wan-2.2 ( 0.7% ) and HunyuanVideo ( 1.5% ) suffer a complete collapse in this discriminative task, likely due to a lack of instruction-following alignment in their training. 3. Closed-Source Models Dominate Physical Simulation. In the generative domain, Sora-2 leads with an average score of 61.6% , followed closely by Veo-3.1 ( 58.9% ), demonstrating superior capability in simulating complex dynamics. Open-source models lag behind at 42.5% and 41.5% under our automated MLLM evaluation. Interestingly, models consistently perform better in Sociology & Humanities, Sora-2: 65.6%, than in Natural Sciences, Sora-2: 57.7% . This divergence suggests that the rigid, immutable laws of physics governing the real world may present a more formidable challenge for models to internalize than the patterns of social dynamics. 4. Advanced Mimicry vs. True Understanding. By juxtaposing Table 2 and Table 3 , we uncover a critical “Perception-Prediction Gap” that distinguishes advanced mimicry from true understanding. A striking dissonance is observed in open-weights models like Wan-2.2 , which achieves a respectable competency in Implicit Generative Action ( 41.5% ) despite a near-zero score in Explicit Understanding ( 0.7% ). This implies that such models operate via statistical pixel mimicry, rendering the texture of causal events without comprehending the underlying logic. In contrast, Sora-2 demonstrates a synchronized profile (Explicit: 51.2% , Implicit: 61.6% ). This correlation suggests that as models scale towards authentic “World Simulators,” their generative actions become increasingly grounded in an explicit grasp of causal laws, marking the transition from surface-level synthesis to physically consistent simulation. Furthermore, while the 5 × 8 5\times 8 layout benefits short clips, it lacks the necessary temporal resolution required for complex causal reasoning in longer sequences. ❷ Implicit Generative Action (1 vs. 4 vs. 7 vs. 10 Pics): As shown in Figure 8 , comparing the results confirms that 7-pics represent the optimal prompt, outperforming both sparse (1, 4 pics) and dense (10 pics) inputs. The lower scores at fewer frames suggest Motion Ambiguity , where the model lacks sufficient temporal vectors to extrapolate future states. Conversely, the slight decline at 10 frames points to Contextual Redundancy where highly compressed keyframes introduce spatial noise that overwhelms the visual encoder’s semantic feature extraction. In summary, these findings confirm that our chosen configurations ( 7 × 10 7\times 10 grid and 7 frames) strike the optimal balance between preserving spatial fidelity and encoding sufficient temporal dynamics required for robust simulation. 4. Related Work Towards “Thinking with Video”. Recent advancements in Video Generation Model have evolved beyond high-fidelity texture synthesis toward complex spatiotemporal dynamics modeling ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ) . This progression supports the conceptualization of video generators as nascent general world simulators and promotes the “thinking with video” paradigm, where generation functions as an intrinsic component of reasoning ( Tong et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025b ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . However, distinguishing genuine causal understanding from mere statistical memorization remains a pivotal challenge, as traditional metrics disproportionately favor perceptual fidelity over logical consistency. The Gap in Existing Reasoning Benchmarks. Emerging benchmarks evaluate various reasoning facets, ranging from rule-based dynamics ( He et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) to open-ended visual reasoning ( Qin et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) and specific tasks ( Yang et al., 2025a ) . While recent efforts attempt to mitigate appearance biases ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Deng, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Cai et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . However, relying on rudimentary tasks, they fail to verify physical and social dynamics. By evaluating discrimination and generation in isolation, they overlook the gap between surface-level outputs and genuine causal understanding. To address the critical gap in current causal evaluation and in contrast to existing methods, we introduce the Causal–Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ) framework. Unlike previous works, CGDJ jointly evaluates internal consistency through two complementary modalities, Explicit Causal Understanding and Implicit Generative Action . By constructing the Causal–Generative Evaluation Benchmark, we provide a rigorous testbed to distinguish whether video generative models have genuinely internalized the physical laws and causal structures governing the scenes they render. 5. Conclusions We redefine reasoning with video generative models as Thinking in Video and introduce the Causal-Generative Dual-Judge ( CGDJ ) to evaluate whether current generators can support this paradigm. By jointly examining Explicit Causal Perception and Implicit Generative Prediction , we reveal a clear Perception-Prediction Gap : models may generate plausible visual dynamics without reliable causal perception, while stronger systems show early but limited alignment between reasoning and generation. We further identify audio-visual misalignment, where verbalized causal knowledge does not necessarily translate into consistent video rollouts. Ultimately, CGDJ advocates shifting video generation evaluation from perceptual fidelity toward causal consistency, offering diagnostic insights for grounded, reasoning-capable world models.
